blocks.text: An **attack surface** is the set of points through which an attacker can interact with a system. Objective 2.4 does not ask you to run a scan: it asks you to **spot weaknesses before an attack** and name their exact category.
Unsupported, Unpatched, Obsolete, and Unmanaged Systems

head: Term
Meaning
Typical Consequence
rows: Unsupported product
The vendor no longer provides any support or patches
No remediation available
Unpatched system
Patches exist but have not been applied
Exploitation of a known CVE
Obsolete system
Outdated technology, replaced by a newer version
Incompatibility with modern protocols, legacy dependencies
Unmanaged system
Outside inventory, outside management and monitoring tools
No one knows it exists or patches it

blocks.note: Unsupported products, patches, and unmanaged systems (pp. 159-164)

blocks.text: Four very close terms: **unsupported** = no more vendor support; **unpatched** = patch available but not applied; **obsolete** = outdated; **unmanaged** = invisible to tools. The answer depends on the keyword in the scenario.
Ports, Services, Operating System, and Virtualization

items: **Ports and services**: every open port is an exposed interface; a forgotten service (e.g., SMB, RDP) widens the surface.
**OS-based vulnerabilities**: kernel, system services, local privileges, default settings.
**Virtualization vulnerabilities**: hypervisor, unpatched VMs, lateral movement between guests, sandbox escape.
**Zero-day**: flaw unknown to the vendor with no patch — no scan detects it, hence the importance of behavioral defense.
**Cryptographic vulnerabilities**: weak algorithms (MD5, SHA-1, 3DES), short keys, obsolete TLS, poor key management.

blocks.note: Exposed services, virtualization, and network hardening (printed pp. 81-83)
What we are protecting and asset exposure (printed p. 15)

blocks.text: Application and Code: The Race Between Check and Use

blocks.field: The system checks a state (time-of-check) then uses it later (time-of-use); the attacker modifies the state in between to bypass the control.

blocks.note: Official objectives — race conditions, TOC, and TOU absent from the 4 books

blocks.text: Race conditions, **time-of-check**, and **time-of-use** are required in §2.4 but absent from the provided books. Classic example: a file verified as safe then replaced before it is opened (TOCTOU).

blocks.field: Password, API key, or token written directly into code or configuration: accessible to anyone who reads the repository or binary.

blocks.note: Hardcoded secrets and credential management in code (printed pp. 96-97)

items: **Malicious update**: a compromised update distributed through the legitimate channel — major supply chain risk.
**Unsafe exception handling**: verbose error messages that reveal paths, queries, or credentials.
**Hardcoded secrets**: to be replaced by a secrets vault and rotation.

blocks.note: Code defects and security review (printed pp. 102-105)

blocks.text: A zero-day cannot be fixed with a patch: respond with surface reduction, compensating controls, segmentation, and behavioral detection.

blocks.q: A script verifies that a file is authorized, then opens it one second later; the attacker replaces it in between. Which vulnerability?
blocks.explain: The gap between verification and use is exploited: this is a race condition (TOCTOU).

items: Unsupported ≠ unpatched ≠ obsolete ≠ unmanaged: four distinct states.
Ports, OS, virtualization, zero-day, and weak crypto widen the system surface.
TOC/TOU is an objectives gap: check then use modified in between.
Hardcoded secrets, malicious updates, and verbose exceptions are code weaknesses.

title: Modern Surfaces: Identity, Configuration, Wireless, LLM, and Public Storage

blocks.text: The modern attack surface is no longer limited to servers: it includes **forgotten credentials**, **unmanaged devices**, **shadow IT**, **connected objects**, **language models**, and **public repositories**.

head: Surface
Concrete Risk
rows: Unmanaged / stale credentials
Forgotten accounts, unrotated service credentials: persistent access for the attacker.
Rogue devices
Unauthorized device plugged into the network (WiFi Pineapple, Raspberry Pi).
Shadow IT
Service or application used without security validation, outside inventory and monitoring.
Misconfiguration
Public bucket, open port, excessive permission, unchanged default value.

blocks.note: Shadow IT and uninventoried assets (printed p. 145)
Network configuration and unmanaged devices (printed pp. 143-145)

blocks.field: Central service that authenticates users and issues tokens to applications (SSO, federation). Critical surface: its compromise grants access to all connected applications.
Apps, permissions, network, local storage, and MDM: an unmanaged work phone combines identity, data, and connectivity.

blocks.note: Official objectives — IdP, mobile, and modern surfaces absent from the 4 books

blocks.text: Identity providers, mobile devices, LLMs, public repositories, and public object storage are **required in §2.4** but not covered by the provided books. They are written from the official objectives.

Wireless networks and low-power protocols (IoT, BLE, Zigbee) add a surface that is hard to inventory: rogue access points, WPS enabled, weak encryption, unmanaged devices. Segmentation and radio inventory are the key controls.

items: **Large language models (LLMs)**: prompt injection, data leakage in responses, dependency on plugins — the surface is the conversational interface itself.
**Public repositories**: public code repository exposing secrets, an API key, or internal system structure.
**Public object storage**: S3 bucket or object storage accessible without authentication, often due to a simple configuration error.

blocks.chapter: Select and Collect the Right Data
blocks.note: Exposed data and asset visibility (printed p. 205)

blocks.text: In a "public bucket" or "API key in GitHub" scenario, look for **misconfiguration** and **public repository / public object storage** — not zero-day or malware.

blocks.q: A developer publishes a GitHub repository containing a valid API key. Which attack surface category?
blocks.explain: The public repository exposes a hardcoded secret: this is a modern public repository surface.

items: Identity: stale credentials, rogue devices, shadow IT, IdP, and mobile are surfaces in their own right.
Misconfiguration is the most common cause of exposure (public bucket, excessive permissions).
Wireless and low-power: rogue access points and uninventoried devices.
LLMs, public repositories, and public object storage are gaps: §2.4 objectives only.
